tier_reason: Peer-reviewed ACM TOMS 47(1) 2020 paper (author copy opened) compares ArborX single-threaded against Boost.Geometry.Index 1.67.0 (packing R-tree) and nanoflann 3b2065e on a named CPU (Xeon E5-2695 v4), and the repo holds a Boost R-tree benchmark backend (benchmarks/bvh_driver/bvh_driver.cpp, backend 'rtree'); the paper states no compiler or flags, so it is not A.

corrections.baseline: Boost.Geometry.Index R-tree (packing/bulk-load algorithm, Boost 1.67.0) and nanoflann kd-tree (hash 3b2065e)
corrections.workload: Section 3.2 of the ACM TOMS 2020 paper: single-threaded tree construction, k=10 nearest search and radius (spatial) search with m = n source/target points from 10^4 to 10^7, for a filled case (filled sphere queries in a filled cube) and a hollow case (hollow sphere in hollow cube), ArborX BVH vs Boost.Geometry.Index packing R-tree and nanoflann; Google Benchmark median, run on one core of a CADES node.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Figures 5 and 6 plot speedup relative to nanoflann (bars read by eye, single thread). Filled case: construction ArborX about 0.85x-1.37x vs Boost about 0.87x-1.32x (similar); nearest search ArborX about 0.58x-0.78x at 10^4-10^6 and about 1.48x at 10^7, Boost about 0.55x-0.93x, so ArborX is about 1.6x faster than Boost at 10^7 (derived from page data). Hollow case: nearest search ArborX about 0.95x, 1.75x, 2.0x, 2.6x at 10^4-10^7 vs Boost about 0.62x-1.22x, so about 2.1x over Boost at 10^7 (derived from page data); construction ArborX about 0.87x-1.12x vs Boost about 1.02x-1.40x, i.e. Boost builds faster in the hollow case. Paper text: 'ArborX and Boost.Geometry.Index libraries perform similarly' for construction; for nearest search 'ArborX significantly outperforms both Boost.Geometry.Index and nanoflann libraries for larger numbers of objects, particularly for the hollow case.'
corrections.hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2695 v4 (18 cores, 2.1 GHz; CADES node, one thread used for the library comparison); scaling runs on OLCF Summit (2x IBM POWER9, NVIDIA V100)
corrections.caveats: Wins are single-threaded and modest: construction is on par with Boost (Boost is faster in the hollow case), ArborX is slower than nanoflann for nearest search in the filled case up to 10^6 points, and the clear win (about 1.6x-2.1x over Boost, derived from bars read by eye) appears only for nearest search at 10^7 points; spatial search in the hollow case at 10^6-10^7 favors Boost over ArborX's 2P variant. Numbers are bar charts with no table. The paper states no compiler, flags or Kokkos version; Boost 1.67.0 and nanoflann 3b2065e are from 2018-2019. The repo's bvh_driver keeps a Boost R-tree backend but no nanoflann backend. ArborX's main value is multithreaded and GPU search (Kokkos), which Boost and nanoflann do not offer.

notes: Paper read from the first author's GitHub Pages repo via raw.githubusercontent.com (arxiv.org, deepai.org and pith.science are blocked). Metadata confirmed on github.com: BSD-3-Clause, 242 stars, 47 forks, not fork/archived, last commit 2026-09-16.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed SIGMOD 2025 paper (PACMMOD 3(1), cited in the README) with public harnesses (tests/cgal.cpp, tests/rtree.cpp, script/run_*.sh), Release flags -O3 -mcx16 -march=native in CMakeLists.txt and first-party raw results in script/data/*.csv; the paper could not be opened and no opened page names the CPU model, so not A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Repo raw results (script/data, times presumably in seconds, hardware unstated), all ratios derived from page data: build.csv, 10^9 3-D points: CGAL kd-tree 1082.4 vs Pkd-tree 3.91 (uniform, about 277x) and 381.3 vs 4.77 (Varden, about 80x). knn.csv, 10^9 3-D points, k=10: CGAL 0.223 vs 0.162 (uniform, about 1.4x) and 3.066 vs 1.713 (Varden, about 1.8x). summary.csv, 10^8 12-D points: build 112.18 vs 0.938 (uniform, about 120x) and 46.69 vs 1.07 (Varden, about 44x); 10% batch insert 171.2 vs 0.115 and 10% delete 29.99 vs 0.148 (uniform); range query 109.1 vs 17.4 (uniform, about 6.3x); kNN column 63.7 vs 51.4 (uniform) but 0.046 vs 0.048 on Varden (CGAL slightly faster). insert.csv/delete.csv: CGAL needs 709-2794 for any batch insert (it rebuilds the tree), and CGAL deletion of 0.1M points takes 0.347 vs 0.0054 (uniform) and 0.033 vs 0.0062 (Varden). Paper numbers seen only in search-result summaries, not checked: 17.4-40.7x faster insertions and 3.27-21.7x faster deletions than Log-tree; on 96 cores 91.9-115x faster construction than the sequential Boost R-tree, 10.4-14.8x faster kNN and 4.13-4.17x faster range report.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: -O3 -mcx16 -march=native (CMakeLists.txt Release build); README: tested with clang 17, also compiles with g++ 13; the compiler used for the paper runs was not confirmed
corrections.stars_or_usage: 90 stars, 4 forks; SIGMOD 2025 (PACMMOD 3(1)) artifact; README says the code now lives in ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib (PSI-Lib)
corrections.caveats: The SIGMOD 2025 paper (doi 10.1145/3709712, arXiv 2411.09275) could not be opened (arxiv.org and cs.ucr.edu blocked), so paper numbers and the CPU model (a search summary says four-way Xeon Gold 6252, 96 cores) are unverified. Comparisons are parallel Pkd-tree against CGAL built with Parallel_tag (TBB) and parallel TBB queries, which is fair for build and query, but CGAL's kd-tree has no batch insert (the harness inserts then rebuilds) and deletes one point at a time, so the huge update ratios reflect a missing CGAL feature. The Boost baseline at HEAD (tests/rtree.cpp) is a 2-D bgi::rtree with quadratic<2> node capacity (a very small node size) built and updated sequentially while Pkd-tree uses all cores; its kNN queries run in a parlay parallel_for. The repo CSVs name no hardware or date. CGAL is slightly faster for one 12-D Varden kNN row. The README says this repository will no longer be updated; the maintained code is ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib.

notes: Kept at B: peer-reviewed venue confirmed via the README citation; opening the paper would likely make it A since code and flags are public. Metadata confirmed on github.com: MIT, 90 stars, 4 forks, last commit 2026-08-20 (README edit). The successor ucrparlay/SpaceTreeLib (PSI-Lib, MIT) is a possible new lead.

tier_reason: First-party README headline (24x multi-thread, 7x single-thread vs GeoPandas) and a per-operation speedup chart image, with no dataset, hardware, thread count, compiler or benchmark script.

corrections.caveats: The baseline is GeoPandas, a Python wrapper over Shapely/GEOS. Arctern's CPU path is built on GDAL/OGR (cpp/src/gis/gdal), which itself relies on GEOS for most predicates, so much of the gain is probably batch processing without per-geometry Python overhead plus multi-threading rather than a faster geometry algorithm. Dataset, hardware, thread count, compiler and flags are not stated (CMake Release uses -O3), and per-operation numbers exist only in a chart image: multi-thread bars range from about 2.3x (geom_equals) and 3.9x (geometry_type) to about 61x (is_simple), single-thread geom_equals is about 0.6x (slower than GeoPandas), and multi-thread intersection is slightly below single-thread. The 36x GPU figure is against Arctern's own CPU code. No comparison with GEOS called directly from C++. Dormant since 2020-06-23 (v0.2.0).

notes: README quotes and chart readings match (average bars about 23.9x multi-thread and 7.2x single-thread). Metadata confirmed on github.com: Apache-2.0, 103 stars, 49 forks, not archived, last commit 2020-06-23.
